questions.stem: A planner asks you to explain why a solenoid in a street signal cabinet has a north pole at one end and a south pole at the other.

answer.exemplar: A current-carrying solenoid acts as an electromagnet. Each turn is a small loop whose north pole lies on the side from which the current circulates anticlockwise, so the contributions of all the turns add along the axis of the coil and the interior field runs from the south end to the north end. questions.explanation: The direction follows from the right-hand rule applied to the current in each turn, which adds along the axis. Stating the grip rule or the pole of a single loop identifies the north end.
questions.hint: Curl your fingers along the current.

questions.stem: A memo asks you to explain why the magnetic force on a charged particle depends on the angle between its velocity and the field.

answer.exemplar: The magnetic force has magnitude q v B sin theta, so it vanishes when the particle moves along the field and is largest when it moves across it. A particle travelling parallel to the field feels no magnetic force at all, because no component of its velocity cuts the field lines. This is why a beam sent down the axis of a uniform field is undeflected while the same beam across the field is bent into an arc.

questions.explanation: Only the component of velocity perpendicular to the field produces a force, which is why the sine of the angle appears. Parallel motion gives no force while perpendicular motion gives the full q v B.

questions.learningObjective: explain how the field of a straight current changes with distance
questions.stem: A survey team asks you to explain how the magnetic field around a long straight underground cable changes with distance from the cable.

answer.exemplar: The field of a long straight wire falls off as one over r, so B equals mu I over two pi r. Doubling the distance from the cable therefore halves the field, while tripling the distance reduces it to a third of its original value. Because the field is strong close in but weak further away, cables carrying large currents must be kept well separated, and the field circles the cable in the sense given by the right-hand rule.

questions.explanation: The field of a long straight current is proportional to one over the distance, so it weakens steadily as you move out. Its direction also circles the wire, changing with the side you stand on.
questions.hint: The field falls as one over distance.

options.text: The force acts along the conductor in the direction of the current
options.misconception: believes the force acts along the wire

options.text: The force is proportional to the square of the current in the conductor
options.misconception: believes the force scales with current squared

options.text: The force is proportional to the current and perpendicular to the magnetic field
The force is zero because the conductor is electrically neutral overall
options.misconception: believes neutrality cancels the magnetic force

questions.explanation: The force is I L B sin theta, so it is proportional to the current and perpendicular to both the field and the wire. Electrical neutrality is irrelevant, since the moving carriers produce the effect.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: predict the change in solenoid field when the current changes
questions.stem: A memo says a solenoid's field inside is 8.0 millitesla at a current of 2.0 amperes. By what factor does the field change if the current is raised to 6.0 amperes?
questions.explanation: The solenoid field is proportional to the current at fixed turn density, so raising the current from 2.0 to 6.0 amperes triples the field. That takes the field from 8.0 to 24 millitesla.
questions.hint: Field scales with current alone.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: explain how to find the force direction for a moving charge
questions.stem: Planners in the depot ask you to explain how to find the direction of the force on a positive charge moving through a magnetic field.

answer.exemplar: Point your right thumb along the velocity of the positive charge and your curled fingers along the magnetic field, then the force points along your extended palm in the direction your fingers push it. If the charge is negative the force is reversed. A useful check is that the three directions, velocity, field and force, are mutually perpendicular, and for a positive charge the triple product v cross B gives the force direction.

questions.explanation: The right-hand rule for positive charges uses the velocity, the field and the force in that order, and negative charges reverse the result. The three directions must be mutually perpendicular.
questions.hint: Velocity, field, force in that order.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: explain how the force direction reveals the current direction
questions.stem: Line engineers are asked to explain how the force on a current-carrying cable tells you which way the current is flowing.

answer.exemplar: The force on a straight current has magnitude I L B sin theta, and its direction is found with the right-hand rule: point your thumb along the current and your fingers along the field, and the force pushes out of the palm. If the force direction is known from the way the cable moves, that rule can be run backwards to deduce the current direction, which is the principle behind motors and moving coil meters.

questions.explanation: The force direction and the current direction are linked by the right-hand rule, so knowing one fixes the other. The magnitude also depends on the sine of the angle between wire and field.
questions.hint: Use the right-hand rule with thumb along current.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: explain why more turns strengthen a solenoid field
questions.stem: A note asks whether increasing the number of turns in a solenoid raises the field inside it while the current stays the same.

answer.exemplar: The field inside a long solenoid is B equals mu n I, where n is the number of turns per unit length. Adding turns to a fixed length therefore increases n and the field rises in proportion, with no change in the current or in the wire. Doubling the turns on the same coil doubles the field, which is why series windings are used to strengthen signal relays and contactors.

questions.explanation: The solenoid field depends on the turn density n, not on the current alone, so more turns per metre means a stronger field. The current and the wire size are unchanged in that comparison.
questions.hint: The formula uses turns per metre.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.learningObjective: explain why the field around a cable forms circles
questions.stem: A surveyor asks you to explain why the field around a cable is directed in circles around the cable rather than along it.

answer.exemplar: A current sets up a field that curls around the wire, because the right-hand rule for a straight current gives a circular field centred on the cable. Each turn of that circle is a closed loop, so the field lines never start or finish and never point along the conductor. The sense of circulation follows the current: point your thumb along the current and your fingers curl the way the field points.

questions.explanation: The field of a current is circular because the right-hand rule wraps it around the conductor. Field lines are closed loops, which is why no field lines begin or end on a straight wire.
questions.hint: Right-hand rule wraps the field around.
